title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a preregistered descriptive summary, explicitly label one‑sided tests as exploratory (they were not prespecified), and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations offers operational gains but introduces safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that degrade correctness for code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our precise research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions (validation and at‑most‑one repair) so that any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and explicit interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair reused by both arms). (3) Transparent reporting of the preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) that did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625), accompanied by preregistered descriptive summaries (paired bootstrap CI = [0.001, 0.01], bootstrap_seed = 1729) and explicit labeling of post‑hoc one‑sided tests as exploratory.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑generated structured outputs are prone to hallucination and prompt sensitivity that materially impact downstream correctness; surveys and controlled experiments document these phenomena across code and configuration domains [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning reduce syntactic/executable errors in several structured domains, though much evidence originates outside NetOps and thus depends on validator/tool fidelity when transferred to networking [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system work emphasizes verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance/proof‑carrying proposals to mitigate automation risks; these works present prototypes and argue that operational reliability depends on validator coverage and externally enforced protocols rather than on any single model alone [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements this literature by preregistering a paired comparison whose estimand isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions. This avoids conflating downstream interventions with first‑pass prompt/decoding differences and clarifies the contribution and limits of validation+repair layers under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation; the preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest is ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec. Key preregistered elements: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. The archived generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate means both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate; the guarded pipeline may reject the candidate via deterministic validation and may invoke at most one permitted repair call. Under this design, paired outcome differences can only arise from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repairs. The design therefore does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, alternative prompts, or constrained decoding arms that were not executed.

Models, validator, and runtime caveat. Declared provider/model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Validator/digital‑twin: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0), which deterministically enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and emits a binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0.

Task corpus and selection. Tasks were selected deterministically using the preregistered ordinal rule producing exactly 1000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). The validator compares parsed candidates against manifest constraints in the digital twin and returns structured traces archived per episode.

Execution accounting, retries, and missingness. The preregistration limited retries (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1) and prespecified missingness treatments. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}. The primary analysis used the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' treatment; sensitivity analyses treating failures as unsafe were preregistered and run when relevant.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed all planned episodes: planned = 2000, completed = 2000, complete_pairs = 1000, failed episodes = 0. Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair calls = 5). Deterministic reconciliation checks passed and contamination/exclusion rules flagged no prompt leakage.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold, so preregistered H1 is not supported.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries and sensitivity. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. This bootstrap interval was preregistered as descriptive only. Mechanistic diagnostics show five validator‑triggered repairs; representative archived validator traces illustrate repair cases where the initial candidate violated required_sequence or touched protected fields and was accepted after the single permitted repair. Total model calls used = 1005.

Why the bootstrap CI may exclude zero while the prespecified two‑sided McNemar is not significant. Exact McNemar uses the discrete distribution of discordant pairs (n10,n01) and, with the observed (5,0), yields a two‑sided p = 0.0625. The bootstrap percentile CI was computed by resampling paired outcomes (with replacement) and estimating the paired difference distribution; with extremely sparse discordant counts, bootstrap resamples can produce nonzero lower bounds even though the exact paired hypothesis test fails to reject at α = 0.05. The preregistered analysis plan treated the McNemar test as the confirmatory procedure and the bootstrap interval as a descriptive supplement; the archival record therefore preserves the inferential hierarchy and the sensitivity explanation above.
sections.discussion:
Inferential hierarchy and interpretation. We emphasize that the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the confirmatory inference: p = 0.0625 and H1 is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary; its exclusion of zero reflects bootstrap sensitivity in regimes with very few discordant pairs and does not overturn the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. Any one‑sided McNemar reported (p = 0.03125) is exploratory/post‑hoc because the preregistration did not specify one‑sided testing.

Mechanistic implications under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the initial candidate was identical across arms for each task, any paired improvements must derive from deterministic validator decisions and the permitted single repair call. The five observed repairs show that a validator covering ordering and protected‑field rules can prevent a small number of unsafe proposals. However, the small repair count constrains inference about the broader efficacy of repair across failure modes and the guarded pipeline would likely have a different measurable effect if (a) baseline failure prevalence were higher, (b) generator semantics allowed independent first‑pass differences, or (c) the repair budget were larger.

Threats to validity. Construct validity: measured safe‑deploy depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; omitted semantic checks would inflate apparent success. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate isolates downstream effects but intentionally precludes measuring first‑pass prompt/decoding interventions. External validity: the synthetic corpus and single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization to heterogeneous production environments and other models. Conclusion validity: extreme baseline success (99.5%) produced sparse discordant counts and reduced power for the preregistered exact paired test relative to the original power assumptions (which targeted baseline≈0.60).

Recommended preregistered follow‑ups. (1) Run an unshared (independent) generation arm to measure prompt/decoding and model‑sampling effects. (2) Sweep repair budgets (0..k repairs) and measure marginal repair returns per failure class. (3) Expand validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity. (4) Evaluate multiple model families to map model dependence. Each follow‑up should preregister power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1005. The primary inferential outcome is the preregistered exact McNemar result; any directional or one‑sided interpretation is exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration. Artifact‑grounded evidence indicates that downstream validator/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. Full preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to support reproducibility and to guide preregistered follow‑ups.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
